entities.name: Gospel of Peter
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Gospel of Peter, a non-canonical text attributed to the Apostle Peter, emerged in the early second century CE, likely within the context of the burgeoning Christian communities in the eastern Mediterranean. This gospel, composed in Koine Greek, represents a unique narrative of Jesus's passion and resurrection, diverging significantly from the canonical accounts, particularly in its portrayal of events surrounding the crucifixion. Its initial acceptance among early Christians was overshadowed by its eventual classification as apocryphal by influential church councils, particularly at Carthage in 397 CE and Rome in 382 CE, which sought to solidify the New Testament canon and establish orthodoxy within a rapidly diversifying religious landscape.

The rediscovery of the Gospel of Peter in the late 19th century in Egypt, specifically in the ruins of a monastery, sparked renewed scholarly interest and debate over its contents. The text recounts the resurrection of Jesus through a distinctive lens, featuring a talking cross and a dramatic portrayal of the resurrection. Such elements highlight the theological diversity that characterized early Christianity, illuminating the struggles for doctrinal authority and the processes of canon formation. This gospel's rejection and subsequent obscurity underscore the tensions between differing interpretations of Christian doctrine in the formative years of the faith.

The legacy of the Gospel of Peter is profound, influencing theological discourse on the nature of resurrection and the role of apocryphal texts in understanding early Christianity. Its existence contributed to the broader narrative of how certain texts were deemed sacred while others were marginalized, shaping the contours of Christian orthodoxy. The ongoing academic interest in this text has spurred discussions about the fluidity of religious texts and the implications of their interpretations throughout history.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Gospel of Peter is an early Christian apocryphal gospel of which a significant fragment was discovered in 1886–87 at Akhmim in Upper Egypt — an eighth-century parchment codex (the Akhmim Fragment, or Codex Panopolitanus) containing approximately 60 verses covering the trial, crucifixion, burial, guard at the tomb, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The text is noteworthy as the only non-canonical source to include a dramatic narration of the actual moment of the Resurrection — in which two gigantic angels descend, open the tomb, and lead out Jesus (whose head reaches to the clouds), followed by a speaking cross — a visionary scene absent from all four canonical Gospels, which record only the empty tomb and post-resurrection appearances. First mentioned by Serapion of Antioch (c. 200 CE), who condemned it as docetic (teaching that Jesus only appeared to suffer), the Gospel of Peter is usually dated to the mid-2nd century CE, with some scholars arguing for an early 1st-century origin.

The docetic quality identified by Serapion — and debated by modern scholars — appears in the text's description of Jesus's silence during crucifixion ('He was silent, as though having no pain') and possibly in the variant of Jesus's last words ('My power, my power, why have you forsaken me?').
